stories.body:
Entertainer and children’s author David Walliams is alleged to have used his fame to approach teenage girls, in some cases reportedly initiating sexual contact with them. Walliams has denied the allegations , but the claims raise some familiar tropes about grooming: why did she go, why didn’t she say no, why didn’t she tell anyone?

After a legal battle, ITV News and The Guardian have now published the findings of a three-year investigation into Walliams, reporting allegations that date back to 2003.

In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce.

Many people imagine sexual grooming as a recognisable and clearly staged process. Build friendship, then trust, then secrecy – all leading towards the offender’s ultimate goal of sexual gratification. But if this were the case, victims could notice the steps and walk away.

Along with a colleague, I undertook linguistic analysis of real chatroom conversations between convicted offenders and adult volunteers posing as 12 to 14-year-old girls. The conversations were made public by the now defunct organisation Perverted Justice, whose activity led to the apprehension and conviction of the offenders. In our analysis, we did not find the pattern mentioned above.

We identified 14 recurring “moves” – parts of the offenders’ language that have particular functions. These include building rapport (for instance by sharing personal stories), assessing risk by checking parents’ schedules or the presence of a boyfriend, escalating sexual topics and planning offline meetings. But these moves overlapped and repeated, with no typical structure emerging.

Rather, offenders seemed to tailor their grooming styles, perhaps according to their individual goals and who they believed they were talking to.

Trust and rapport

What was consistent was the large amount of rapport-building, which often ran through the whole interaction. Grooming research invariably shows that rapport-building and trust development are the central devices used to persuade and manipulate.

This may be through compliments, sharing personal information and declarations of trust. Grooming strategies are designed to develop intimacy and trust, isolate the victim and dismantle the “red flags” that might alert them to the manipulative nature of the conversation. Trust development makes it much harder for victims to notice devious intentions – there is no obvious point at which the young person has failed to spot something plainly visible.

Offenders in our data spent much of their conversations sizing up their targets. They would try to work out whether a target was likely to engage, suited their preferences, was accessible and unlikely to expose them. We called this a “risk-reward ratio assessment” – in other words, a judgement about whether this person was worth their effort.

In another study , we examined the case of an offender who took a scattergun approach, in this case targeting nearly 1,000 potential young victims. This individual would strategically cycle through an array of fake online personas to identify the one most likely to “hook” his target. The vast majority ignored or rejected his first advance, at which point they were dropped. But this is the point of the scattergun approach; a small percentage, usually the most vulnerable, will respond.

Our work also revealed how offenders manage the risk of being caught. For many we studied, a key strategy was to use language that shifted responsibility on to the target.

Questions were often formulated to elicit sexually explicit content by positioning the target as the one in control. The groomer might say, for example, “how far do you want to go”, “tell me what you wanna do”. This phrasing both presumes interest and makes declining more difficult, while laying the groundwork to say later that the young person had led the conversation.

Another feature was what we termed the “mitigating lol”. This could be something like “u should send me a nude vid lol”. This served to reduce the impact of a sexual question by implying playfulness. It also supports future claims that the requests was insincere – possibly a useful tactic in a trial. We can only infer the purpose, but it points to the same strategy of building in deniability.

I cannot speak directly to the Walliams allegations, but when it comes to celebrities in general, the task of building trust and rapport may well be easier. The victims already feel they know them, and are made to feel special by being approached. It’s also easy to see how the perks of celebrity could do much of the persuasive work.

A widely used definition of grooming across linguistics and psychology describes preparing the child, their significant adults and the wider environment for abuse. Compliance and secrecy are explicit goals. They are not evidence of the victim’s character.

So when people ask, “why did they keep replying?” or “why did they go to the house?” they are asking why a technique that was designed to engage did in fact keep them engaged. When we ask, “why didn’t they tell anyone?” we are questioning why a strategy engineered to cultivate silence did exactly that.

Grooming involves a complex network of strategies. But we know it is never the young person’s behaviour that’s the problem. The “perfect victim” who resists every advance and raises the alarm at every opportunity is a myth.

Better understanding of the strategies can help caregivers, educators and children to recognise grooming earlier. It should also shape what we say to victims after the fact. Let’s stop asking why they gave their email address, why they went to the house, why they didn’t tell anyone. Let’s question instead the actions of those responsible.

stories.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents

stories.body:
The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.

In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.”

It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.”

But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office.

They are not just numbers.

Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.

Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica.

“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.”

In their own neighborhood

Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan

In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status.

Both she and her brother are citizens.

“Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.”

DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.

As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.

DHS denies that they were ever detained.

“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.”

On her way to work

Andrea Velez

In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.

“Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.”

Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.

After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside.

At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant

Quentin Williams

In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building.

Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe.

“They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.

Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours.

Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.

Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.”

Attending a horse race

Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children

In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children . Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens.

Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.

Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”

She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.”

On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. When Tello refused to exit the car without her younger siblings, agents pulled her so roughly out of the car that she fell, leaving bruises. She said agents zip-tied her hands.

Romero and Tello said the agents refused to remove the zip ties for hours, despite Tello’s age. The teenager said the incident has affected her view of law enforcement. Her mother says that the 6-year-old still has nightmares. Officers are meant “to keep us safe,” Tello said. “But yet they treated all of us like that.”

John Carter was working security at the track when the raid started. He had brought his girlfriend and his two children along with him. He recalls officers throwing a flash-bang near him and his son, and then the officers detained them. “They cinched the zip ties down as tight as they could,” Carter said. He said the officers also zip-tied his 14-year-old daughter but removed the restraints when he complained.

Carter explained that he is active in the local Republican Party and a strong supporter of law enforcement. But he said that what he saw officers doing that day was wrong.

“Things are supposed to be done humanely and correctly,” he said. “This wasn’t.”

The agents also detained Juana Rodriguez, who attended the event with her family. She said that she was zip-tied beside her 3-year-old son, which left her unable to pick him up and comfort him during the long hours they waited to prove their citizenship. “He wanted me to hug him, to hold him,” Rodriguez said. She and her son are both U.S. citizens and lead plaintiffs in an ACLU of Idaho lawsuit alleging the raid illegally targeted Latinos. ICE, the FBI and several Idaho agencies have denied the charge and asked that the lawsuit be dismissed.

DHS did not respond to any specific allegations made by Rodriguez, Romero, Carter or their families. Instead, a spokesperson wrote in an email statement that the raid successfully helped dismantle an illegal gambling operation, and that ICE officers “didn’t zip tie, restrain or arrest any children.” The FBI declined to comment to ProPublica but told local media no “young children” were zip-tied. DHS, the FBI and multiple Idaho law enforcement agencies have refused to share the number of U.S. citizens held that day.

“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself.”

Monitoring ICE operations

Amanda Trebach

In August 2025, Amanda Trebach, a nurse and volunteer with an immigrant advocacy organization, said she was monitoring ICE activities outside a facility that the agency was using to stage operations when agents grabbed her and pinned her to the ground, kneeling on her neck and back . They shoved her into the back of a van and held her for several hours until taking her to a federal detention facility in Los Angeles. She was not given the opportunity to speak with an attorney during the 33 hours that she was in custody. She said agents took her phone and never returned it.

DHS said Trebach was detained because she attempted to physically impede its agents’ operations by jumping in front of moving vehicles, hitting their cars with her protest signs and shouting obscenities at agents. She denies this.

She said that after the incident she felt paranoid that she was being followed.

“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in the dark by myself,” she said. “I didn’t know if they were going to come get me.”

Driving to work

George Retes

George Retes, a U.S. Army veteran who served in Iraq, was driving into work at a cannabis farm in July 2025 and arrived to find the place being raided by immigration agents. Protesters had gathered outside the farm. He found himself trapped between the agents and the protesters. The agents broke his car window, pepper-sprayed him and pulled him out onto the ground. He was detained for three days, missing his daughter’s third birthday. Retes said, agents refused to explain why he’d been detained or to let him call relatives or a lawyer.

When ProPublica published Retes’ story last year, he said agents knew he was a citizen.

“They didn’t care,” he recalled. “They still sent me away to jail.”

DHS officials made statements claiming Retes had assaulted their agents. But he was never charged.

Working at his auto shop

Javier Ramirez

In June 2025, immigration agents conducted a raid on an auto shop owned by Javier Ramirez and his family. He said agents swept him up as they were detaining his workers. He recalled hearing one of the agents yell: “Hey, just get him! He’s Mexican.” He said agents tackled him and one of them put a knee on his face. He recalled hearing the agents boasting about the numbers of immigrants they were detaining across the city that day, saying: “How many did you get? I got 10, I got 15.” According to a lawsuit that Ramirez filed against DHS, he said he was held in federal custody for four days and was denied medication he needs for diabetes. DHS has not filed a response to the lawsuit, but previously the agency said that Ramirez was arrested for obstructing law enforcement, and that it never denied him medication.

“I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’”

Working at his car wash

Rafie Ollah Shouhed

Rafie Ollah Shouhed, 79, was born in Iran, moved to Los Angeles after the Islamic Revolution and became a U.S. citizen. On Sept. 9, 2025, Shouhed, owner of Valley Car Wash, watched with alarm as immigration agents stormed into his business and attempted to detain his employees. He rushed outside to see what was going on. Security video of the incident shows agents knocked Shouhed to the ground repeatedly. He told agents that he had just had heart surgery. “They were sitting on me,” he recalled. “I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’” He said in an ongoing lawsuit that the agents kept him handcuffed for 12 hours and left him with injuries to his arm, elbows and ribs. Shouhed said that he’s still receiving treatment for his injuries, and that he has quit working. DHS said Shouhed was arrested for interfering with and assaulting officers and did not answer questions about his lawsuit. He was released without charges.

Monitoring ICE operations

Jeane Wong

When Jeane “Bleu” Wong, an operator of a daycare center and activist, heard in July 2025 that ICE agents had arrived at a nearby apartment complex, she rushed to the scene to provide assistance to people who were being detained. Agents detained her when she tried to remove one of their masks.

She was held in the San Ysidro Port of Entry , the largest and busiest land border crossing in the Western Hemisphere, and later moved to a federal prison. Wong said that during her time in custody she was strip-searched and shackled in chains that restricted her from using the restroom. Federal authorities charged Wong with assaulting a federal agent. She eventually pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.

A little over a year later, Wong received a notice from the California Department of Social Services that her license to care for children had been revoked because of the assault. She and her wife are selling their home and relocating outside of Southern California.

“We could totally fight, and I’d probably win,” she said. “But we don’t have the money, time, energy.”

Working construction

Leonardo Garcia Venegas

Leonardo Garcia Venegas was laying concrete with his construction crew in Alabama in May 2025 when immigration agents arrived at the site without a warrant and began detaining his co-workers, including his brother. Garcia Venegas pulled out his phone to film the agents. Videos he and other workers recorded show agents approaching to arrest Garcia Venegas while he filmed, tackling and arresting him while he yelled that he was a U.S. citizen. Garcia Venegas said that he told the agents he had his REAL ID on him, but that they dismissed the document as fake. They held him in handcuffs for an hour before finally releasing him without charges. DHS said he was impeding officers. After that first incident, immigration agents detained Garcia Venegas two more times, each time ignoring statements and identification documents that prove he is a U.S. citizen.

Garcia Venegas filed a lawsuit against DHS over its warrantless raids on construction sites. DHS responded to the lawsuit, saying that its agents didn’t need warrants to operate at construction sites because they’re open to the public. The agency also said that brief stops like Garcia Venegas’ were “reasonable.” Until the case is resolved, a judge ordered a temporary halt to the operations.

“I just want to live in peace,” he told ProPublica after his third arrest .

“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship.”

Driving to the doctor

Aliya Rahman

Aliya Rahman, who is autistic and disabled, was driving to a doctor’s appointment in January when she reached an intersection where protesters were confronting immigration officers. She said several agents swarmed her car and yelled at her to move out of the way. They broke her window and pulled her from the car.

“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship,” Rahman said.

DHS said agents detained Rahman because she ignored their instructions. She denied that, saying that she was confused and saw no way to move without hitting someone.

She said agents then shackled her feet and held her in a detention cell at the federal building. She passed out and awoke in a hospital room. She was released without charges later that day.

Sleeping in her bedroom

Jeyli Salguero

In January, Jeyli Salguero awoke when she heard someone banging on her door and then the sound of the door breaking open. Federal agents, their guns drawn, rushed inside and told her family they were looking for her brother.

“We told them yes he lived here, but he doesn’t live here anymore,” Salguero said she told the agents. “They started getting a bit more angry and were like, ‘Since you’re not collaborating, we’re gonna start checking your status.’” An agent grabbed Salguero’s phone and ordered Salguero to face a wall. In an ongoing lawsuit, Salguero has said that the agents entered the home without a valid warrant. DHS said that agents were searching for a fugitive, and that it has suspended the policy of entering homes without a judicial warrant.

Her father has temporary protected status but had not received paperwork showing that his status had been renewed. He was handcuffed and then detained for a month. Salguero’s older sister, who was undocumented, was handcuffed and deported to El Salvador. The rest of her family is now planning to sell their home and move to El Salvador. “It’s been a mental toll — a very big mental toll on all of us.”

Protesting the Broadview ICE Detention Center

Juan Muñoz

Juan Muñoz, an elected member of the Board of Trustees that governs Oak Park Township outside of Chicago, was participating in an October protest outside the Broadview ICE Detention Center when he said that he was knocked to the ground by the commander of the Border Patrol. “When I looked up,” Muñoz recalled, “it was Commander Greg Bovino who was standing over me.” In depositions, Bovino denied tackling Muñoz, saying videos of the arrests showed no “reportable uses of force.”

Muñoz said agents knocked away his phone and zip-tied his hands. “Every agent that I encountered, I told the same thing, ‘I’m an elected official.’ No response.”

Muñoz was held inside of the detention center for eight hours before agents dropped him off at a gas station, without explaining why he’d been held. “They were over capacity, keeping people for way longer than that facility was intended for,” he recalled about the detention center. “It was filthy. They don’t have proper hygiene products or are able to feed people properly,” Muñoz said. DHS did not comment on his specific detention. But, referring to Muñoz and other protesters detained with him, it posted a comment on social media, saying, “We will NOT allow violent activists to lay hands on our law enforcement.”

Responding to ICE in a hospital

Jessie Fuentes

In October 2025, Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes said she rushed to a local emergency room because she’d been told that ICE agents had been spotted inside. She identified herself to the agents as an elected official and began asking them whether they’d obtained a warrant. Video taken of the incident shows that agents grabbed and handcuffed her. Fuentes was held for 15 minutes, during which time members of her staff posted the video online and her supporters gathered outside the hospital to demand her release. DHS, in a written statement, told ProPublica that Fuentes was put in “handcuffs but NEVER placed under arrest.”

“These individuals are operating above the law,” Fuentes said. “They’re operating with impunity.”

Monitoring ICE operations

Caitlin Arwen

Caitlin Arwen was scrolling through a Facebook group for moms in October when she noticed a shared post that said immigration agents were detaining people in her town, which is about an hour’s drive outside of Chicago. Later that day she saw some of the vehicles that had been posted on Facebook and began following them, honking her horn to alert residents of their presence. One of the vehicles slammed on its brakes. U.S. marshals who were working with ICE surrounded her car, broke her window and pulled her out.

“They threw me on the broken glass, and they were all on top of me. I couldn’t breathe,” she recalled. Arwen estimates she was kept handcuffed face down on broken glass for roughly 35 minutes. “They taunted me, took photos of me, called me names, berated me and acted like I was somehow deserving of this.” DHS referred questions about Arwen’s arrest to the U.S. Marshals Service. A spokesperson for the service said Arwen’s arrest was a “task force arrest” and declined further comment.

Arwen was taken to a hospital, where marshals handcuffed her to the bed. After she was discharged, agents shackled her and moved her to a DHS detention facility, where she was not allowed to contact a lawyer or anyone else for help. “I didn’t have access to water or food the whole time,” said Arwen, adding that she was held for several hours. “Nobody showed me their badge all day. No one identified themselves. No one once read me my Miranda rights.”

Though federal officials declined to prosecute Arwen, state authorities charged her with traffic violations and obstruction of law enforcement. She has pleaded not guilty.

stories.title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
stories.summary: The post A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
After the midterm, a Republican member of the election board in Forsyth County, Georgia, challenged dozens of ballots using information from a controversial data tool created by a member of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network.

Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting their ballots.

The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.

But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.

The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats swept statewide offices .

The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been central to his push to assert greater federal control over voting .

In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed suspicious.

ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.

Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its capacity to help GOP candidates contest their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who lose.”

The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to “citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a recording reviewed by ProPublica.

Read More

In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond to questions from ProPublica.

Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.

“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for what they want to.”

Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.

In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches involving people with the same names.

Voting rights groups have called ELLY error-prone . The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as dead .

State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica, explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”

Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director. Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than 22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as their first name.

During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so officials could investigate further.

But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for” Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to you and having you submit it.”

Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for the data’s accuracy.

“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100% correct,” he said.

The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the matter.

Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there. One said the person lived in Arizona .

ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive.

Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested — and why.

“It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it first,” she said.

Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned.

In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said.

The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.”

The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial.

One voter, Alexander Knight, told ProPublica that he goes by his middle name and that the information in voter records mirrors how Department of Driver Services officials suggested he be identified on his driver’s license.

“I am real,” he told ProPublica.

Four other challenged voters said they, too, abbreviated their first names. A. Joseph Guntherberg confirmed he routinely used the same formulation of his name, adding that blocking his ballot would not help the challengers: “My candidate didn’t win.”

Richards said it was up to county election workers to check ELLY’s data — he merely gathers it to facilitate efforts to maintain accurate voter lists.

But at the meeting, Joel Natt, a Republican board member, said the responsibility lay with challengers to justify their accusations. “This has no relevance to anybody here until” they provide solid evidence, he said, “through the proper channel.”

stories.title: Power Shift: State Election Wins Open Path for Climate Progress
stories.summary: In the U.S. midterm elections, Democrats won control of governorships and state legislatures across the country. At a time of public outcry over data centers and rising electricity costs, incoming leaders will have a mandate to rein in polluters, constrain utilities, and advance clean energy. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Keisha Lance Bottoms, governor-elect of Georgia, celebrating her victory in Atlanta on election night. Paras Griffin / Getty Images

OPINION

In the U.S. midterm elections, Democrats won control of governorships and state legislatures across the country. At a time of public outcry over data centers and rising electricity costs, incoming leaders will have a mandate to rein in polluters, constrain utilities, and advance clean energy.

By Michael Gerrard • November 12, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

After their sweeping victories in the midterm elections, Democrats will control both houses of Congress, meaning they will be able to shape the budget, conduct vigorous oversight and investigations, and refuse to confirm nominees for judgeships and other high positions — but their power will be limited. Any ambitious new bill to tackle climate change, for example, will face President Trump’s veto pen.

But there are other ways for Democrats to make progress on climate, energy, and the environment — by wielding their newfound power in the states. In the November 3 elections, Democrats flipped control of governors’ offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas, and are on track to win in Alaska, where votes are still being counted. They also attained trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both houses of the state legislature — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin.

This brings to 29 or 30 the number of states that will have Democratic governors in January, and to 22 the states in which Democrats have unified control of government. Meanwhile, Republican trifectas were broken in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.

While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation. Public outcry over the growth of data centers, which are driving ever more burning of natural gas, and the rising cost of electricity mean that Democrats have a mandate to advance energy reforms in the states they control.

By one estimate, tech companies are intent on spending more than $647 billion over the coming years to develop natural gas infrastructure in the U.S. to serve the voracious power demands of data centers. The planned expansions would grow the existing fleet of gas generators by roughly two-thirds. Natural gas is already the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. (behind petroleum, but far greater than coal), and this investment would lock in its use for decades.

Against this backdrop, public opposition to data centers has rocketed. In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one. In her successful campaign for governor of Texas, which is facing the largest natural gas buildout in the nation, Gina Hinojosa pledged an immediate moratorium on new data centers. Many other winning candidates also promised more controls on data center construction.

State-level results of the 2026 midterm elections. States “flipped” where Democrats attained a governorship or a trifecta, meaning control of the governorship and both houses of the state legislature. Votes in the Alaska and Kansas gubernatorial races are still being counted, but at press time, Democrats lead in the vote totals. (Nebraska is labeled as having a trifecta, but it has a unicameral legislature.) Yale Environment 360 / Made with Flourish

Looking ahead, governors have the opportunity to appoint regulators who will further rein in data centers and the power utilities profiting from rising energy prices. Retail electricity rates are set by state public utility commissions, and in 38 states the commissioners are named by the governors. The newly elected Democratic governors of Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Maine all campaigned on promises to appoint commissioners who would work to favor the interests of ratepayers over those of monopoly utilities.

In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers. It could also mean encouraging more rooftop and community solar to help lower electric bills. Utilities have long campaigned against such projects, which cut into their profits.

In Georgia, where commissioners are elected, Democrats just won a majority of seats on the five-member commission, promising greater scrutiny of the utilities. In Pennsylvania, legislation to lower power bills by reducing utility profits recently stalled in the Republican-controlled state senate, but under the new Democratic trifecta, this legislation is expected to be signed into law. In Michigan, about 80 percent of voters approved a ballot measure that will block utilities from campaign spending (which the utilities are already challenging in court). And in Colorado, voters rejected a ballot measure, championed by gas utilities, that would have established a “right to natural gas” and blocked local moves to phase out gas appliances.

Most federal environmental laws set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment. The Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry, has long consisted of three Republican members. A Democrat won election to the body with a platform that included capping orphan wells and banning gas flaring — two important means of stemming emissions from drilling. He can now put these issues on the agenda. His election also makes it possible for Democrats to win control of the commission in 2028.

Democratic candidates for state attorney general triumphed over Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas. Republican attorneys general have been at the forefront of litigation aimed at weakening environmental regulations, and they have moved in concert to protect oil and gas companies from being held accountable for climate damages. These states are expected to reverse their positions in many cases, which might tilt the scales in some.

What else might Democrats do with all their new power?

Given the focus of almost all campaigns on affordability, not many states are likely to adopt measures that would transparently increase consumer costs, such as a tax on carbon. However, states have many other tools. Most federal environmental statutes, such as the Clean Air Act, set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Demonstrators protest outside a forum for congressional candidates in Peekskill, New York, in October. Adam Gray / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Of the 10 states that burn the most coal for power, Democrats will now control the governor’s office in seven: Texas, Kentucky, Illinois, Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia, and Iowa. Governors in those states have considerable ability to shut coal plants down, for example, by setting air pollution standards that are too expensive for plants to meet.

If coal plants are to be shuttered and the use of natural gas slashed, the nation will need much more renewable energy, particularly wind and solar, to meet its growing electricity demand. One way to ramp up wind and solar is through renewable portfolio standards, which require utilities to acquire a certain percentage of their power from renewable sources. Today, 27 states have such standards, but many are so low that they have already been met. Democratic wins mean that more states can adopt renewable portfolio standards or strengthen and enforce those already on the books.

State leaders can also clear roadblocks for new renewable energy development. Over the last 30 years, more than 850 cities and counties have adopted restrictions on wind and solar, often spurred on by residents’ objections to large renewable installations proposed in their communities. In response, several states have adopted laws that centralize authority over such facilities, allowing them to override local bans. New York’s law has been especially successful at boosting wind and solar installations. Other states that now have Democratic trifectas could adopt similar laws.

States can encourage the uptake of electric vehicles by building more charging stations and providing rebates to EV buyers.

States may also encourage household solar by making it easier for homeowners to obtain approvals for rooftop arrays; enabling net metering; legalizing balcony solar; easing the siting of battery storage systems; and facilitating virtual power plants, which allow energy companies to link together and control home batteries, solar panels, thermostats, and other assets to balance the grid.

While states cannot require citizens to buy electric vehicles, they may encourage their uptake by building more charging stations, requiring new parking lots and garages to install fast chargers, and providing rebates to EV buyers to offset the recent loss of federal subsidies.

States can reduce emissions from the residential sector by incentivizing the installation of heat pumps, strengthening energy efficiency standards for buildings, and — though federal courts are split on whether this is permissible — barring new natural gas hookups.

These measures are only a fraction of what states can do. The Model Climate Laws Initiative, a joint project of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law and Environmental Advocates NY, has posted more than 2,000 model and actual state and local laws, and it stands ready to draft many more. Thoughtful policies aimed at cutting power bills, curbing pollution, and advancing clean energy have been circulating for a long time. It is time to put those policies into action.

stories.title: The False Promise of Pakistan’s Military
stories.summary: Washington should rethink its relationship with the generals. The post The False Promise of Pakistan’s Military appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Vice President JD Vance (C) walks with Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir (L), and Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar after arriving for talks with Iranian officials on April 11, 2026 at Islamabad, Pakistan. (Jacquelyn Martin - Pool/Getty Images)

Ever since Pakistan emerged as a mediator between Iran and the United States, Pakistan’s military chief, General Asim Munir, has been praised in Washington for being a statesman and a reliable security partner. President Trump has repeatedly called him his “favorite field marshal .”

Washington has made this bet before, and lost.

For decades, successive U.S. administrations supported Pakistan’s military rulers to advance their geopolitical agendas, overlooking—and at times reinforcing—authoritarianism in exchange for stability and cooperation.

The Trump administration is repeating the same bargain. It has defined counterterrorism, critical minerals, and managing regional competition with China among core U.S. interests. And yet, each of these is threatened by the very institution the United States has relied on to preserve them. The Democratic-controlled Congress now has an opportunity to reverse course.

Previously, the United States justified its support of the Pakistani military because it was perceived as a strong institution with widespread domestic support. Its legitimacy has eroded considerably since the ouster of former Prime Minister Imran Khan through a no-confidence vote in 2022. Many analysts believe that the military, after falling out with Khan, withdrew its backing and paved the way for his removal. A significant segment of the public turned against an institution long deemed untouchable.

For the United States to continue its support of Pakistan’s military risks its long-term relationship with a population of 250 million people, two-thirds of whom are under 30 and increasingly restless under growing military authoritarianism.

The problem directly affects Washington’s security interests.

The Pakistani military’s record as a counterterrorism partner should give Washington pause. Following 9/11, the military received billions of dollars in U.S. taxpayer money to combat the Taliban and al-Qaeda. Twenty years later, the Afghan Taliban returned to power, in part due to the Pakistani military’s patronage and protection of various Afghan Taliban factions within Pakistan.

This is not simply a story of past failure. Even today, the Pakistani military dominates counterterrorism policy in Pakistan’s two most restive provinces: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) and Balochistan. The military’s predominant use of coercive measures— mass displacements , drone warfare , and military operations in KPK—has failed to stem militancy and has instead caused widespread civilian suffering .

Balochistan, one of Pakistan’s most resource-rich provinces, has been racked by unrest and violence for decades. As in KPK, security policy in Balochistan is under the strict control of the military, with heavy army and Frontier Corps deployments.

Rather than take seriously the legitimate grievances of the people—failed governance, abysmal human development indicators, resource exploitation without local input or benefit—the Pakistani military has resorted to enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings , and detentions of Baloch students and activists. Earlier this year, Mahrang Baloch, a Nobel Peace Prize nominee who has led a peaceful movement for Baloch rights, was sentenced to life in prison in a secret trial.

In both provinces, militant violence has soared over the past two years.

The pervasive instability in Balochistan, in particular, threatens another major American interest: critical minerals, an essential part of the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy. In early 2026, the U.S. Export-Import Bank approved financing of $1.25 billion to support the mining of critical minerals at Reko Diq, home to one of the world’s largest untapped gold and copper deposits, located in the Chagai district of Balochistan.

However, increasing militancy in the province has exposed this investment to considerable risk and has already delayed the start of the project. Rather than learn from the Chinese experience—where billions of dollars of investments in Balochistan have foundered because of insecurity—the U.S. risks repeating it.

There is another contradiction in Washington’s approach.

For years, the United States saw Pakistan firmly in China’s orbit. In his second term, President Trump attempted to shift that approach and rebuild ties with the Pakistani military in order to preserve some measure of influence.

However, the Pakistani military is not just a security partner, it is the principal architect of Pakistan’s China policy. It manages defense acquisitions, economic projects, and the overall strategic relationship between the two countries.

That relationship continues to deepen. Following the India-Pakistan conflict in May 2025 in which Pakistan made effective use of Chinese technology and weapons, Pakistan’s defense budget increased by 20 percent. China, Pakistan’s largest arms supplier, stands to benefit from that expansion.

By building relations with the Pakistani military, the United States is not preserving influence. Rather, it is strengthening the very institution responsible for deepening ties with China.

An institution with little civilian oversight and accountability has little incentive to recalibrate a security paradigm that has allowed it to maintain its central and privileged relationship with the United States.

The United States holds significant influence over how its support is used: approval of F-16 sustainment sales, training through the IMET program, access to international financial systems, and diplomatic cover. It should condition that support on measurable human rights benchmarks, starting with the release of political prisoners, an end to military trials of civilians, and accountability for enforced disappearances. Such standards are rooted in Pakistan’s own constitution and its international commitments.

Democratic control of the House and Senate gives Congress an opportunity to reverse the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan’s military. Over the past two years, more than 100 Democrats in Congress signed letters calling out the Pakistani government’s human rights violations. Now, as incoming chairs of powerful committees, they can hold hearings, attach conditions to appropriations and defense bills, and investigate the Trump family’s crypto deals with foreign governments, including Pakistan’s.

Washington cannot determine Pakistan’s political future, nor should it try. But it can refuse to let American taxpayer dollars, military cooperation, and diplomatic backing prop up an increasingly unaccountable military establishment. Washington can keep treating Field Marshal Asim Munir as a security partner, even though his rule has not delivered stability. Or, instead of enabling military authoritarianism, it can recognize that America’s long-term interests lie in strengthening the civilian rule that Pakistanis have repeatedly voted for.

stories.title: End-Stage Trumpism
stories.summary: Over the next two years, Congress and the lower courts will try to do what they can to prevent Trump from burning down the house. The post End-Stage Trumpism appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

The Democratic Party’s blowout in the midterm elections has generated a number of obituaries for Trumpism. Trump himself still has two years left in his term, but the press has begun to treat him, too, as a “dead man walking.” At 80 years old, he has no political future after the next 24 months, unless you count his lifetime appointment to the Board of Peace. This explains his fixation on legacy, whether he measures that in spurious peace deals, catastrophic attempts to effect regime change, or grandiose building projects around Washington, DC.

Trumpism is another matter. It’s a personality cult, so it’s hard to imagine that it will survive for long without Trump at its helm. On the other hand, Stalinism remains powerful in Russia today, despite the unimaginable horrors associated with his reign. And Fujimorism is alive and well in Peru, despite the conviction, jailing, and death of right-wing founder Alberto Fujimori. In July, his daughter Keiko became president of the country after several unsuccessful bids for the office. Eric, Donald Jr., and Barron are probably scanning the relevant Wikipedia pages on Peru to nurture their own dreams.

Trump has comparable ambitions to cast a long shadow over his country’s future. And that’s why the next two years will be perilous ones. It would be bad enough if the president focused only on expanding his personal wealth at the expense of the republic or on remodeling Washington DC at the expense of its residents. Infinitely worse are the consequences of Trump trying to cement his legacy by forcing a punishing peace upon Ukraine, turning Iran into a huge crater, and/or triggering regime change in Cuba.

Along the way, Trump will defy Congress by continuing to prop up the fossil fuel sector and deport as many people as possible from the United States. Together with his newly minted chief-of-staff Stephen Miller, the president will attempt to destroy what little faith American citizens still have in the idea of government by gutting agencies, eviscerating critical government services, and putting the least competent people into key roles (I’m looking at you, Pete Hegseth).

In matters big and small, Trump will spend the next two years acting like a derelict renter who has decided to trash his place of residence out of anger, pettiness, and vengeance. Congress and the lower courts will try to do what they can to prevent him from burning down the house. But Trump, an accomplished pyromaniac, is holding all the matches. His opponents, alas, deploy only the thinnest of firehoses.

Can the voters who communicated their views so forcefully in the midterms do anything in the next two years to limit the damage and prepare for regime change at home in 2028? Let’s first look at the potential for mayhem in Trump’s foreign policy.

Iran and Cuba

It’s no surprise that an uber-narcissist like Donald Trump has an ego problem. He has pursued foreign policy goals largely to demonstrate that he can cut through the Gordian knots that bedeviled earlier presidents. Sure, he wants a Nobel Peace Prize. But he also has a long-shot desire to top the list of America’s best presidents.

In his first term, Trump surprised everyone by reaching out to North Korea’s Kim Jong Un. Addressing North Korea’s nuclear program promised no economic dividends for himself or his family. Sitting down with an authoritarian leader of a country with one of the worst human rights records in the world won him no points with his Republican allies, given that the country lacks oil and lucrative investment opportunities.

No, the reason Trump zeroed in on North Korea was because his predecessors—particularly Bill Clinton and Barack Obama—had failed to prevent North Korea from going nuclear. Resolving that particular geopolitical problem was equivalent to purchasing a distressed property that had cycled through several unsuccessful owners and turning it into a luxury hotel.

Trump’s fixation on Iran follows a similar script. One of his first acts in office in 2017 was to rip up Obama’s deal with Iran and promise a more effective substitute. Trump thought that Benjamin Netanyahu was offering a deal of a lifetime earlier this year to do Obama one better by removing the Iranian regime from power.

But the resulting war has only made matters worse by revealing U.S. military and geopolitical weaknesses. Suddenly, it turned out, the Pentagon didn’t have enough weapons to get the job done or keep the energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. Since power in an age of deterrence relies heavily on perception, the optics of these U.S. failures are very bad indeed.

This kind of impulsive, hubristic decision—to wage war on a significant military power that can quickly restrict the flow of fossil fuels—has marked Trump’s style from the beginning. This time, however, it cost his party its control of Congress.

Trump continues to vacillate between a desire to visit retribution upon Iran and the hope of achieving a big peace deal that would justify the war. The administration has readied an attack plan that “would likely go beyond efforts to simply ‘mow the lawn’ or maintain the status quo by striking radars, launchers and other Iranian assets that can be quickly reconstituted,” reports CNN. Although details of the plan have not leaked to the press, Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT), who called it “insane” after receiving a confidential Pentagon briefing.

Since the election, however, Trump has waxed more conciliatory. He has touted the current negotiations with Tehran—much as he has played up negotiations in the past—and has promised to hold off on any strikes as long as Iran is committed to making progress .

But Trump faces some structural impediments. He is not a patient man, and diplomacy requires patience. To achieve a deal, he also needs able negotiators. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff simply don’t know enough to negotiate a nuclear deal with Iran. Finally, Trump is desperate to reduce gas prices, and Iran knows that it has the U.S. president over a barrel (literally).

Trump hates one thing above all: losing. He doesn’t want to lose at war or at peace. To avoid either result, he might prefer to spend the next two years in a state of sporadic conflict with Iran rather than accept a losing verdict.

Trump’s fixation on winning, until he took on Iran, explained his preference for grabbing at low hanging fruit. He has claimed to resolve wars that weren’t even ongoing, like the conflict between Egypt and Ethiopia. He conducted a raid to seize Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro—against a relatively weak military—and didn’t bother with the heavier lift of regime change. He has bullied weaker parties—Ukraine, Greenland, Colombia—in order to get his way.

With stronger adversaries, like Russia and China, Trump has rolled out the red carpet. His general approach has been to punch down and toady up.

This approach may impel him to turn next to Cuba, where he has combined an economic pressure campaign (tightening an energy blockade) with a Venezuela-like cultivation of an insider (Raul Castro’s grandson, nicknamed “the Crab”). Since neither of these strategies has panned out, the administration has turned to a perverse form of crowd-sourcing.

Last month, the CIA posted on social media a Spanish-language solicitation to snitches along with a quote from Secretary of State Marco Rubio: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba — now is the time. The disappointment of failed promises, corruption and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”

Here, too, Trump hopes to trump his predecessors. The Bay of Pigs debacle hung over the presidency of John F. Kennedy much as the Iran hostage crisis doomed the presidency of Jimmy Carter. By tackling these intractable conflicts in his last two years, Trump hopes he can one-two punch his way above both Carter and Kennedy in the presidential rankings. Good luck with that.

Then There’s Ukraine

Among the countries that have disappointed Trump, none ranks higher than Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky refused to serve as Trump’s servant by digging up dirt on Joe Biden’s son or promote the conspiracy theory that Ukraine, not Russia, interfered in the 2016 elections. Zelensky then had the temerity to challenge Trump’s tenuous grasp on modern history in a public appearance at the White House. And those pesky Ukrainians continue to refuse to acknowledge that Russia is bigger and stronger—and accordingly surrender their land and sovereignty to the bully next door.

Democratic control of Congress might jumpstart an effort to restore aid to Ukraine. In the meantime, Trump will no doubt continue to believe that his personal touch—and relationship with his soulmate, Vladimir Putin—will produce a “big, beautiful” deal on European security, including an agreement on Ukraine. Downgrading NATO and welcoming Russia back into the European fold is only the latest Trump effort to brown-nose Putin back to the negotiating table.

It doesn’t seem to matter to Trump that no one shares his opinion on such a deal. The Ukrainians have not been part of negotiating the terms. The Europeans don’t seem to know the details. Even the Russians have expressed some skepticism .

The talks this week in Abu Dhabi focused instead on small, grubby deals —more micro-ceasefires like the one secured for Oleshky, another agreement covering grain shipments out of the Black Sea—but managed only to achieve a prisoner exchange. No grander agreements are likely when Putin believes that he can press his air superiority and bomb Ukraine into submission. Ukraine, meanwhile, has blocked Russia’s advance on the ground and inflicted over 50,000 casualties in October. It is truly a punishing stalemate.

Trump has a couple months before the new Congress takes office and pushes U.S. policy back in the direction of Ukraine. But because Putin hopes to use General Winter to subdue Ukraine, Trump is basically shouting into the wind. Just as Henry Kissinger turned an opening with China into personal profit, Trump salivates at what he could accomplish by ending the war in Ukraine and midwifing a raft of corrupt business deals with Putin and his family of oligarchs. He’s willing to give Putin just about anything to make this wish come true. But the Kremlin is not a Make-a-Wish foundation, far from it.

Distracting Trump

In action movies, when a crazy shooter is holed up in a difficult-to-reach spot, the police will deploy a dangerous tactic. They’ll pop up in open areas to draw the shooter’s fire. By distracting his attention in the front, other law enforcement officers can sneak around back to catch him unawares.

Trump is obsessed with vengeance. So, over the next two years, it will be necessary to distract his attention from the big, terrible things he could do by drawing his ire with pesky lawsuits, investigations, and civic challenges. That’s what Congress can do, and Democrats might find common cause with enough Republicans to infuriate the president in this fashion.

It’s not so much that such actions can actually tie his hands. Rather, they will rely on Trump’s capacity for tying his own hands. He just can’t resist lashing out at his enemies.

Democracy, after all, is not just about voting. It’s about the power of institutions and processes to limit autocratic actions. Trump has proven that he has no problem ignoring such institutions and processes. But he never backs down from a fight.

So, in the end, democratic actors here can help limit the amount of damage Trump does on the international stage by absorbing his anger and his energies on the home front. It won’t be pretty. Trump, close to his political expiration date, can still be very dangerous. But luring the president into a congressional mud fight will be a lot better than cleaning up the messes he wants to inflict on the rest of the world.

The even more important task is to go after Trumpism. While Trump focuses on wrestling his opponents—in Congress, in lawsuits, in public pissing contests—everyone else can work behind the scenes on rebuilding democracy. At the state and local level, where Trump allies suffered huge losses, politicians and average citizens of various political stripes can spend the next two years strengthening the institutions that Trump has tried to destroy. Only a true rebirth of democracy can send Trumpism into an irreversible death spiral.
